Recently read that Elon Musk is funding an ethical committee that is supposed to work on AI laws. Perhaps similar to those used in I,Robot.

I can not for the life of me grasp how ethical laws can be successfully implemented in all AI that are developed, as media seems to suggest. My field of study is machine learning and I have yet to even find an algorithm where this can be implemented. The AI is per definition stupid as of now. Most algorithms just attempt to find order in data we see as chaos.

The laws wrongfully assume that AI capable of messing us up is capable of understanding the very laws they're supposed to uphold. They can't. They most likely won't in a very long time. It takes one company with an evil agenda. It takes one developer with a shitty day producing a horrible bug which may not be discovered before it's too late.

I get the ethical idea of attempting to implement such laws. But it is technically impossible to guarantee. It will never be anything more than legalese mumbo jumbo about promising to try to create bots that will never hurt humans.

I would like to see someone prove me wrong on this!
How can AI/Robot laws actually be implemented?

I think an AI's ability to understand or "think" per say, can be compared to that of dimensions. Let's take the example of a robotic hotel bellboy. People get on the elevator every day and they voice a command to tell "it" which floor they want to go to. The programmer of this robot coded it to specifically press a certain button based on the voice interpretation that it has installed. The robot doesn't necessarily know why the person wants to go to a certain floor, it doesn't even know why the person even got on the elevator. All it knows is that it will press a certain button/floor based on the voice command that a customer will give. This is the idea of a robot with a single dimensional understanding of a code. It simply does what it is told without thought. This function is already a part of society today and we see it in computers, smartphones, tvs and even calculators.

 

What's interesting is when this single dimension kicks into a non-linear level, like the second or third. I'll try to refrain from suggesting that each dimension is a level of consciousness of the robot because I simply don't know what the limit is. However, I do not think it would be far stretched to believe that just as our understanding of the world, which most likely began from a primitive, flat 0 dimension, evolved over time and that this, too will happen to robots/AI's as well.

 

For robotic laws, I'll base mine on Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics.

  1. A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.
  2. A robot must obey orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.
  3. A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.  

The first law's wording allows it to be dimensionally flexible. The whole idea of the first law is to protect a human being under any circumstance, including a robot's inaction. When a robot takes in this law, it would have to understand what it means to place a person under “harm”. We humans are annoyingly beautiful in its capacity to understand “harm” as both a physical and emotional phenomenon. A robot’s single dimensioned understanding of “injuring” a human being could see it as a physical reaction, rather than an emotional one. Basically, when a robot see’s you in pain, screaming or knows that you’re about to die – physically, it will do what it can to protect/preserve you. But it won’t know what it means when you are getting bullied or verbally abused (But if you’re showing physical signs of “injury” I guess it could be stretched to encompass that). A robot with a higher level of understanding would be able to interpret this law to a deeper level, like us.

 

The second law is a progression of the first one and it simply brings more depth to robotic laws. Finally, in the third law, what we see here is the acknowledgement that a robot is self-aware of its own safety in Asimov's three laws. Personally, I think we have yet to reach this state, but based on many of the world's powerful leaders such as Musk or Hawking, it isn't too far off. If we were to come up with robotic ethics, it would probably start from the first law, and eventually we would have to add the second and third laws over time. In programming language, the first law would have to be embedded in the very roots of an AI’s birth, and instead of seeing it as a “law” as we do, it would have to see them as a line or multiple lines of code denoting restrictions/guidelines. Try to think of these "laws" that will one day be implemented into AI as that of a scientific law, an inherent truth observed as what it is, unlike a hypothesis or scientific theory.

 

tl;dr: Robots still think one-dimensionally. So the first law of robotics would have to be implemented as a code/string of commands. Eventually, this too will evolve (whether by itself or by us).
